extracted.intended_audience: self-employed taxpayers, employers, payroll/tax professionals, and tax advisors
extracted.subtask_description: Treasury/IRS regulatory guidance defining what counts as a 'qualified tip' eligible for the deduction under Internal Revenue Code section 224, and the reporting, occupation, and limitation rules that govern claiming that deduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualified tip must be voluntarily paid and designated by the payor
rubrics_metrics.description: A qualified tip is an amount voluntarily provided by the payor (customer) as a tip and designated by the payor as such; it must not be compelled by contract terms or recharacterized by the service provider.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: The 10% cash tip Painter G received after services (not in service agreement) is a qualified tip; amounts included in a service contract or otherwise compulsory are not qualified. The amount of the qualified tip is the amount determined by the payor (see Landscaper L example where only the $100 spontaneously given by the customer is a qualified tip).

rubrics_metrics.name: Service charges included in a service contract are not qualified tips
rubrics_metrics.description: A service charge that is included in the service contract before the services are provided, or payment conditioned on such an agreed charge, is not a qualified tip.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Painter G's 15% contractual service charge is not a qualified tip because it was included in the contract and payment of services was conditioned on it. Shuttle Driver S's 20% gratuity included in the contract option is not a qualified tip because it was not voluntary in the sense that declining it would change the contractual price.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended or stated gratuities may be qualified if fully discretionary
rubrics_metrics.description: A recommended or suggested gratuity is a qualified tip if the payor has complete discretion to increase, decrease, or eliminate it entirely with no consequence to the service provided or the price.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: A contract that states a recommended 15% tip that the customer may change or eliminate, and the customer voluntarily pays it after service, qualifies as a tip (Example 9).

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional voluntary amounts added after service completion are qualified tips
rubrics_metrics.description: Amounts added by the payor after the service is completed, provided voluntarily and without compulsion, are qualified tips to the extent they were determined by the payor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Shuttle Driver S receiving an extra $5 after a contracted $60 fare; that $5 is a qualified tip. Similarly, the $100 extra given spontaneously to Landscaper L is a qualified tip (but additional amounts recorded by the provider as 'tips' but actually part of the agreed charge are not).

rubrics_metrics.name: Amounts reclassified by the service provider from the agreed price are not qualified tips
rubrics_metrics.description: If the service provider reclassifies part of the agreed contract price as a 'tip' on its books, that reclassification does not make those amounts qualified tips; they remain part of the charge for services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Landscaper L received $5,100 for a $5,000 contract but recorded $4,500 as installation and $600 as tip; only the $100 actually determined and given by the payor is a qualified tip; the $500 reclassified amount is not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contributions required to access content are payments for services, not tips
rubrics_metrics.description: A contribution that is required to obtain access to content or services (e.g., a required contribution to a platform to access videos) is payment for services and is not a qualified tip.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Digital Content Creator H's $5 required contribution to access locked training videos is a payment for services (not a tip); a later voluntary $2 contribution given as appreciation is a qualified tip.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntary digital contributions may be qualified tips; superficial digital acknowledgments do not change tip nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Voluntary contributions made through digital platforms (including those that display a contributor's comment or highlight the contribution) are qualified tips if not required; superficial or nominal digital tokens of appreciation by the recipient do not alter the contribution's nature as a tip.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Digital Content Creator K's voluntary contributions during a livestream (which may be highlighted in chat or receive a personal thank-you) are qualified tips. The regulation explicitly notes that negligible-value acknowledgments like highlighting a comment or thanking the contributor do not make the contribution non-tip.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualified tips must be reported on an information return or on Form 4137
rubrics_metrics.description: Except as modified by transition rules, qualified tips are eligible for the deduction under section 224 only if included in the amount of cash tips separately reported on a statement furnished to the taxpayer pursuant to specified information-reporting provisions, or reported by the taxpayer on Form 4137 (or successor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited reporting provisions include section 6041(d)(3), 6041A(e)(3), 6050W(f)(2), and 6051(a)(18).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transition rule for tax year 2025 reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: For taxable years beginning before January 1, 2026 (i.e., tax year 2025), qualified tips must be included in the aggregate amount reported on the applicable statements or reported on Form 4137, but cash tips do not need to be separately reported on the statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a temporary relaxation of the separate-line reporting requirement for informational statements for the transition period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statements to sole proprietorships or single‑member LLCs are treated as furnished to the owner
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements furnished to a sole proprietorship or a single‑member LLC that does not elect corporate treatment are considered furnished to the tip‑recipient owner of that entity, regardless of whether the entity's name appears as the recipient on the statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rule clarifies the reporting treatment where the information return names the business rather than the individual owner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade-or-business limitation on deduction for self‑employed tip recipients
rubrics_metrics.description: For qualified tips received in the course of a taxpayer's trade or business (other than employment), the deduction for qualified tips is allowed only to the extent that gross income from that trade or business (including qualified tips) exceeds the sum of deductions allocable to that trade or business (other than the section 224 deduction). The section 224 deduction itself is not counted among those other deductions for this purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This effectively limits a self‑employed taxpayer's section 224 deduction to the net income (before the section 224 deduction) from the relevant trade or business. Examples illustrate situations where gross income minus allocable deductions constrains the deductible amount.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall maximum deduction amount referenced ($25,000 example)
rubrics_metrics.description: The regulation references a maximum deduction amount under section 224 (and paragraph (b)(1) of the section) of $25,000 in its illustrative examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Manicurist M with $30,000 in qualified tips and sufficient net income is permitted to deduct $25,000 because that is the statutory/ regulatory maximum referenced in the examples. (See paragraph (b)(1) for the governing maximum amount.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Social Security number requirement for claiming the deduction
rubrics_metrics.description: To claim a section 224 deduction, the taxpayer must include on the tax return the Social Security number (SSN) of the individual who received the qualified tips; the SSN must have been issued before the tax return due date (including extensions) for the calendar year in which the deduction is claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SSN is defined per section 24(h)(7) of the Code; absence of a timely-issued SSN prevents claiming the deduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Married-filing requirement to claim deduction and SSN rules for spouses
rubrics_metrics.description: Taxpayers who are married (as defined in section 7703) must file a joint return to claim the section 224 deduction. Only the SSN of the taxpayer who received the tips is required to claim the deduction, unless both spouses received qualified tips, in which case SSNs for both are required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This sets filing and identification requirements for married taxpayers seeking the deduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Occupational eligibility: only listed occupations that customarily and regularly received tips on or before Dec 31, 2024 are eligible
rubrics_metrics.description: Only qualified tips received in connection with occupations listed in Table 1 (occupations that customarily and regularly received tips on or before December 31, 2024) are eligible for the section 224 deduction, subject to the other requirements of the statute and regulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Table 1 enumerates multiple TTOC occupation codes and descriptions (e.g., bartenders, wait staff, digital content creators, taxi and rideshare drivers, etc.). Assistants or apprentices are included in an occupation category if they perform the same services described in the occupation entry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipient must be performing duties of a tipped occupation when receiving the tip
rubrics_metrics.description: A tip is eligible only if paid to an individual while performing duties of an occupation that is included in Table 1; tips received while performing non‑tipped duties (or while holding a non‑tipped occupation) are not qualified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Manager M receiving a $5 tip while handling a customer complaint as a restaurant manager (an occupation not in Table 1) is not a qualified tip. If the same manager performs waitstaff duties (an occupation in Table 1) and receives a tip while doing so, that tip is qualified (Example 13 and 14).

rubrics_metrics.name: Termination and applicability dates for the section 224 deduction
rubrics_metrics.description: The deduction is not allowed for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2028, and the regulation applies to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This sets the effective period during which the deduction and these rules apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information reporting changes for independent contractors beginning tax year 2026
rubrics_metrics.description: Historically, independent contractors did not receive information returns that separately reported tips; beginning in tax year 2026, information returns furnished to both independent contractors and employees will separately report certain tips.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Footnote discussion explains prior lack of separate tip reporting on Forms 1099-MISC for independent contractors and the planned change starting in 2026 that will separately report certain tips.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deduction under section 224 does not affect FICA/SECA wage/tax treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Although tips are considered wages for FICA purposes under section 3121(q), the deduction under section 224 does not apply for FICA or SECA purposes and is not taken into account in determining wages subject to FICA or net earnings subject to SECA tax.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Footnote clarifies that the section 224 deduction is distinct from payroll tax treatment; taxpayers should not assume the section 224 deduction reduces wages for FICA/SECA.
